text:
Temperature calibration gives wrong probabilities when labels are not 0..k-1

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I calibrate multiclass models with `CalibratedClassifierCV` and tried the new temperature scaling method on a dataset whose classes are coded 1, 2 and 3. The probabilities looked off compared to sigmoid calibration, so I compared against the same data with the labels shifted to start at 0.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `method="temperature"`, `CalibratedClassifierCV.fit` only label-encodes `y` when its first element is a `str`. Integer labels that are not already `0..n_classes-1` (for example 1/2, -1/1 or 1/2/3) are passed to the temperature fit as raw class indices. The fitted temperatures are then wrong and `predict_proba` changes when the classes are only renamed. There is no error or warning. With labels 1/2 every fold's `beta_` lands on the lower bound of the search, exp(-10), which flattens the calibrated probabilities. String labels give exactly the same result as 0/1, so the bug only affects integer labels outside `0..n_classes-1`. This happens with both `ensemble=True` and `ensemble=False`, and on 1.8 and 1.9, so released versions are affected.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression


def fit_temperature(X, y, ensemble):
    clf = CalibratedClassifierCV(
        LogisticRegression(), method="temperature", cv=3, ensemble=ensemble
    ).fit(X, y)
    betas = [float(c.calibrators[0].beta_) for c in clf.calibrated_classifiers_]
    return np.round(betas, 6), clf.predict_proba(X)


X, y = make_classification(n_samples=60, n_features=4, random_state=0)
X3, y3 = make_classification(
    n_samples=60, n_features=4, n_informative=3, n_redundant=1, n_classes=3, random_state=0
)
problems = {
    "binary": (X, y, {"1/2": y + 1, "-1/1": 2 * y - 1, "str": np.array(["a", "b"])[y]}),
    "3-class": (X3, y3, {"1/2/3": y3 + 1, "str": np.array(["a", "b", "c"])[y3]}),
}

for problem, (Xp, y0, relabelled) in problems.items():
    for ensemble in (True, False):
        ref_betas, ref_proba = fit_temperature(Xp, y0, ensemble)
        print(f"{problem}, ensemble={ensemble}, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = {ref_betas}")
        for name, yr in relabelled.items():
            betas, proba = fit_temperature(Xp, yr, ensemble)
            same = np.allclose(proba, ref_proba)
            print(f"  labels {name:6s}: beta_ = {betas}")
            print(f"    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed {same}, expected True")
print(f"exp(-10) = {np.exp(-10):.6f} (lower bound of the beta search)")
```

### Expected Results

Renaming the classes should not change the calibration: for every relabelling, `beta_` should match the `0..k-1` fit and `predict_proba` should be equal to it (`True` on every line), as it already is for string labels.

### Actual Results

```
binary, ensemble=True, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = [0.740325 0.383557 0.434524]
  labels 1/2   : beta_ = [4.5e-05 4.5e-05 4.5e-05]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels -1/1  : beta_ = [4.500000e-05 1.823720e-01 1.619173e+00]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels str   : beta_ = [0.740325 0.383557 0.434524]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed True, expected True
binary, ensemble=False, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = [0.468948]
  labels 1/2   : beta_ = [4.5e-05]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels -1/1  : beta_ = [0.192596]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels str   : beta_ = [0.468948]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed True, expected True
3-class, ensemble=True, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = [0.878013 0.526881 1.740861]
  labels 1/2/3 : beta_ = [4.500e-05 4.500e-05 5.229e-02]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels str   : beta_ = [0.878013 0.526881 1.740861]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed True, expected True
3-class, ensemble=False, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = [0.842258]
  labels 1/2/3 : beta_ = [4.5e-05]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels str   : beta_ = [0.842258]
    predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed True, expected True
exp(-10) = 0.000045 (lower bound of the beta search)
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026, 10:18:26) [GCC 13.3.0]
executable: <venv>/bin/python
   machine: Linux-7.1.5-76070105-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.1
          pip: None
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.5.4
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: 3.0.6
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
     narwhals: 2.27.1

Built with OpenMP: True
```

OS: Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS. The same code is on main.

### Interest in fixing the bug

The guard is in `CalibratedClassifierCV.fit` (`sklearn/calibration.py` lines 483-487 at 85593ca7a0, line 377 in 1.9.1): `if self.method == "temperature" and isinstance(y[0], str): y = label_encoder_.transform(y=y)`. Temperature scaling came in with #31068 and the guard was last changed in #32246. For integer labels `y` reaches `_TemperatureScaling.fit` unencoded, where `labels = column_or_1d(y, dtype=dtype_)` (line 1205) goes into `HalfMultinomialLoss`. The loss uses the label directly as a column index, `k = int(y_true[i])` and then `raw_prediction[i, k]` (`sklearn/_loss/_loss.pyx.tp` lines 1271-1272). With labels 1/2 the positive class indexes column 2 of a two-column row, and -1 indexes before the row. The extension is built with `wraparound=False` and bounds checks off (`sklearn/meson.build` line 186), so these indices read outside the row instead of raising.

The fix I would propose is to encode `y` whenever `self.method == "temperature"`, dropping the `isinstance(y[0], str)` condition. I tried that change locally on 1.9.1, and `predict_proba` then matches the `0..k-1` result for all the relabellings above with both `ensemble` values. A regression test could check that `predict_proba` does not change when the labels are shifted or remapped, for `ensemble=True` and `ensemble=False`. I am happy to open a PR with the fix and the test.

IterativeImputer(keep_empty_features=True) modifies the input array in place

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for tabular modelling and use `IterativeImputer` with `keep_empty_features=True` so that the output keeps the input's columns.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `keep_empty_features=True`, `IterativeImputer.fit_transform` and `transform` write into the array I pass in. Multimetric scoring mixes up scorers that differ only in pos_label

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for binary classification work and evaluate models with `cross_validate` and `GridSearchCV` using several scorers at once.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When a `scoring` dict contains two scorers that use the same response method but different `pos_label`, for example average precision for class 0 and for class 1, the second scorer silently receives the response computed for the first scorer's `pos_label`. Its scores are wrong, with no error or warning. Scored alone, the same scorer gives the right value. This affects `cross_validate` and anything else that builds a multimetric scorer, such as `GridSearchCV` with a `scoring` dict and a `refit` choice based on those scores. It happens with both `response_method="predict_proba"` and `response_method="decision_function"`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, make_scorer
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.randn(60, 3)
y = (X[:, 0] + 0.5 * rng.randn(60) > 0).astype(int)

for response_method in ("predict_proba", "decision_function"):
    ap_neg = make_scorer(
        average_precision_score, response_method=response_method, pos_label=0
    )
    ap_pos = make_scorer(
        average_precision_score, response_method=response_method, pos_label=1
    )
    clf = LogisticRegression()

    alone = cross_validate(clf, X, y, cv=3, scoring={"ap_pos": ap_pos})
    both = cross_validate(clf, X, y, cv=3, scoring={"ap_neg": ap_neg, "ap_pos": ap_pos})

    print(response_method)
    print("  expected test_ap_pos (ap_pos alone):   ", np.round(alone["test_ap_pos"], 3))
    print("  observed test_ap_pos (with ap_neg too):", np.round(both["test_ap_pos"], 3))
    print("  test_ap_neg:", np.round(both["test_ap_neg"], 3))
```

### Expected Results

`test_ap_pos` is the same whether `ap_pos` is the only scorer or is evaluated together with `ap_neg`:

```
expected test_ap_pos (ap_pos alone):    [0.901 0.965 0.932]
```

### Actual Results

```
predict_proba
  expected test_ap_pos (ap_pos alone):    [0.901 0.965 0.932]
  observed test_ap_pos (with ap_neg too): [0.456 0.379 0.391]
  test_ap_neg: [0.811 0.944 0.893]
decision_function
  expected test_ap_pos (ap_pos alone):    [0.901 0.965 0.932]
  observed test_ap_pos (with ap_neg too): [0.456 0.379 0.391]
  test_ap_neg: [0.811 0.944 0.893]
```

With `ap_neg` in the same dict, `test_ap_pos` drops from about 0.93 to about 0.4 in every fold, for both response methods.

### Versions

### Interest in fixing the bug

The cause is `_cached_call` in `sklearn/metrics/_scorer.py` at 85593ca7a0, lines 92-104. The multimetric cache is keyed on the response method name only, but the value it stores is the output of `_get_response_values(..., pos_label=pos_label)`, which is already specific to `pos_label`: the `predict_proba` column for that class, or `decision_function` with its sign flipped when `pos_label` is the first class. `_Scorer._score` passes each scorer's own `pos_label` (lines 461-466), and `_use_cache` (line 195) enables the cache exactly when two scorers share a response method, so the second scorer gets the first scorer's output. Before #26037 (1.3.0) the cache held the raw method output and each scorer selected its own column afterwards, so this looks like a regression from that change. No test in `sklearn/metrics/tests/test_score_objects.py` combines two scorers that differ only in `pos_label`.

A fix is to key the cache on the pair `(response_method, pos_label)`, or to cache the raw response and apply the `pos_label` selection per scorer after the lookup. I would add a test with two scorers that differ only in `pos_label`, for `predict_proba` and `decision_function`. I am happy to open a PR for this.

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. ### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for tabular modelling and rely on `OrdinalEncoder` with `min_frequency` on columns that also contain missing values.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

For a feature that has both infrequent categories and missing values, `OrdinalEncoder.inverse_transform` decodes the infrequent rows to NaN and the missing rows to `"infrequent_sklearn"`. `transform` is correct, so the round trip silently swaps the two groups with no error or warning. Anything that decodes encoded data back to the original labels, for example to report or inspect predictions per category, gets the wrong labels for those rows.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

# One feature with two frequent categories, one infrequent category and
# two missing values.
X = np.array(["a"] * 5 + ["b"] * 5 + ["c"] + [np.nan] * 2, dtype=object).reshape(-1, 1)

enc = OrdinalEncoder(min_frequency=2).fit(X)
print("categories_:", enc.categories_[0].tolist())
print("infrequent_categories_:", enc.infrequent_categories_[0].tolist())

Xt = enc.transform(X)
print("transform, last 3 rows:", Xt[-3:, 0].tolist())

X_inv = enc.inverse_transform(Xt)
print("observed inverse_transform, last 3 rows:", X_inv[-3:, 0].tolist())
print("expected inverse_transform, last 3 rows:", ["infrequent_sklearn", np.nan, np.nan])
```

### Expected Results

The infrequent row decodes to `"infrequent_sklearn"` and the two missing rows decode to NaN:

```
expected inverse_transform, last 3 rows: ['infrequent_sklearn', nan, nan]
```

### Actual Results

```
categories_: ['a', 'b', 'c', nan]
infrequent_categories_: ['c']
transform, last 3 rows: [2.0, nan, nan]
observed inverse_transform, last 3 rows: [nan, 'infrequent_sklearn', 'infrequent_sklearn']
expected inverse_transform, last 3 rows: ['infrequent_sklearn', nan, nan]
```

`transform` gives the codes 2, NaN, NaN as expected, but `inverse_transform` returns NaN for the `c` row and `infrequent_sklearn` for both missing rows.

### Interest in fixing the bug

The cause is in `sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py` at 85593ca7a0, lines 1640-1658. `inverse_transform` first writes the missing index (3 here, the position of NaN in `categories_[0]`) into the missing rows at line 1643, then computes the infrequent code at line 1650 as `len(categories) - len(infrequent_indices[i])`. `len(categories)` counts the NaN category, but `_fit_infrequent_category_mapping` (lines 369-415) removes the missing category before building the mapping, so `transform` uses one code fewer. Here `inverse_transform` expects the infrequent code to be 3, which is exactly the missing index, so the missing rows are flagged as infrequent and the real infrequent code 2 is decoded through the filtered `categories`, whose last entry is NaN. This logic dates from #25677 (1.3.0) and is the same on 1.9.1. `test_ordinal_encoder_missing_appears_infrequent` in `sklearn/preprocessing/tests/test_encoders.py` only checks `transform`.

A fix is to take the infrequent code from the fitted mapping (`self._default_to_infrequent_mappings[i].max()`, or subtract one when `i in self._missing_indices`) and make sure missing rows still decode to NaN after `categories` is filtered. I would add an `inverse_transform` round trip to the missing-and-infrequent test. I am happy to open a PR for this.

`TargetEncoder.fit_transform` raises `KeyError: 'groups'` when metadata routing is enabled and no `groups` are passed

### Introduce yourself

Dear all,
I am a professor of applied math at École polytechnique, very close to the Turing build, so important for the scikit-learn community. I use scikit-learn mainly for teaching, as the ones doing the hard jobs are now my students.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `enable_metadata_routing=True`, `TargetEncoder.fit_transform(X, y)` raises `KeyError: 'groups'` when it is called without `groups`. This is the common case. It also happens inside a `ColumnTransformer` or a `Pipeline`, so any pipeline that contains a `TargetEncoder` fails as soon as routing is switched on globally. The bug does not depend on the CV splitter: the default `cv=5` and `StratifiedKFold(...)` both fail.

The cause is in `sklearn/preprocessing/_target_encoder.py` (line 366 in 1.9.1, unchanged on `main`):

```python
if _routing_enabled():
    if params["groups"] is not None:
        X, y, params["groups"] = indexable(X, y, params["groups"])
    routed_params = process_routing(self, "fit_transform", **params)
```

`params` only contains the metadata that were actually passed, so `params["groups"]` fails when no `groups` are given.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.choice(["a", "b", "c"], size=(100, 1))
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=100)

TargetEncoder().fit_transform(X, y)
```

### Expected Results

No error. The cross-fitted encoding should be the same as with routing disabled, since there is no metadata to route.

### Actual Results

```
  File ".../sklearn/preprocessing/_target_encoder.py", line 366, in fit_transform
    if params["groups"] is not None:
       ~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^
KeyError: 'groups'
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.14 (main, Sep  1 2026, 14:17:39) [MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)]

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.1
        numpy: 2.5.4
        scipy: 1.18.1
       pandas: 3.0.6
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
     narwhals: 2.27.1
``
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

`Fixing the bug appears to be easy:
Replacing
```python
           if params["groups"] is not None:
```
by
```python
            if params.get("groups") is not None:
```
in File ".../sklearn/preprocessing/_target_encoder.py", line 366.

I will be pleased to help fix this bug, which will be my first commit to scikit-learn.

BUG: HistGradientBoosting merges distinct values at upward-rounded midpoints

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi! I'm a machine learning developer. I use scikit-learn regularly for building predictive models and data analysis.

While researching how tree-based models handle highly separable datasets, I noticed an unexpected drop in accuracy in a specific edge case. I dug into the source code to understand why the model was failing to learn the separation and managed to trace it down to this specific floating-point rounding tie in the binning logic.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

There is a floating-point precision flaw in the HistGradientBoosting binning logic. When the algorithm computes the arithmetic midpoint between two very close, distinct floating-point values, the finite midpoint can round upward to equal the upper data value.

Because the threshold comparison is upper-inclusive (<= threshold), both distinct values are incorrectly lumped into the exact same bin. This prevents perfectly separable targets from being learned by the model.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Here is a minimal reproducer where 20 zeros and 20 ones are perfectly separable, but the model completely fails to distinguish them and predicts 0.5 for everything due to the midpoint rounding tie:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

# Create distinct values separated by a tiny margin
x_base = np.array([1, 2], dtype=np.float64)
x_transformed = 1 + (2**-52) * x_base

# Repeat to satisfy default min_samples_leaf=20
X = np.repeat(x_transformed, 20).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.repeat([0, 1], 20)

# One boosting step with learning_rate=1 should perfectly separate this
model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=1, learning_rate=1.0)
model.fit(X, y)

print("Predictions:", model.predict(X))
```
### Expected Results

The distinct values should be separated into different bins, allowing the tree to split them and predict [0, 1] accurately.

### Actual Results

The midpoint rounds to the upper value, placing both sets of data into bin 0. The model predicts 0.5 for all samples.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.1 and current main
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I am interested in fixing this.

Root cause and strategy: The root cause is that the arithmetic midpoint of two adjacent distinct floats can round upward to precisely equal the upper float. Because the threshold split uses <=, both values are assigned to the same bin. The strategy for the fix is to detect when the computed finite midpoint equals the upper bound and in that specific case, replace the threshold with the lower bound. This mathematically guarantees the values are separated.

I already have a C-level patch and a suite of 84 regression tests prepared locally that successfully implements this strategy. I will wait for this issue to be triaged, but I am ready to open a PR for this as soon as the team approves.

Disclosure: An AI assistant helped me isolate the binary64 rounding mechanism that causes this failure. I have manually verified the math and the failure.

Because the threshold comparison is upper-inclusive (<= threshold), both distinct values are incorrectly lumped into the exact same bin. This prevents perfectly separable targets from being learned by the model.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Here is a minimal reproducer where 20 zeros and 20 ones are perfectly separable, but the model completely fails to distinguish them and predicts 0.5 for everything due to the midpoint rounding tie:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

# Create distinct values separated by a tiny margin
x_base = np.array([1, 2], dtype=np.float64)
x_transformed = 1 + (2**-52) * x_base

# Repeat to satisfy default min_samples_leaf=20
X = np.repeat(x_transformed, 20).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.repeat([0, 1], 20)

# One boosting step with learning_rate=1 should perfectly separate this
model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=1, learning_rate=1.0)
model.fit(X, y)

print("Predictions:", model.predict(X))
```
### Expected Results

The distinct values should be separated into different bins, allowing the tree to split them and predict [0, 1] accurately.

### Actual Results

The midpoint rounds to the upper value, placing both sets of data into bin 0. The model predicts 0.5 for all samples.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.1 and current main
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I am interested in fixing this.

Root cause and strategy: The root cause is that the arithmetic midpoint of two adjacent distinct floats can round upward to precisely equal the upper float. Because the threshold split uses <=, both values are assigned to the same bin. The strategy for the fix is to detect when the computed finite midpoint equals the upper bound and in that specific case, replace the threshold with the lower bound. This mathematically guarantees the values are separated.

I already have a C-level patch and a suite of 84 regression tests prepared locally that successfully implements this strategy. I will wait for this issue to be triaged, but I am ready to open a PR for this as soon as the team approves.

Disclosure: An AI assistant helped me isolate the binary64 rounding mechanism that causes this failure. I have manually verified the math and the failure.

FeatureAgglomeration.inverse_transform fails on list/DataFrame input, including its own set_output result

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I work in AI, ML, DS and use scikit-learn for preprocessing and modeling pipelines, usually with set_output(transform="pandas").

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`FeatureAgglomeration.inverse_transform` indexes its input directly (`X[..., inverse]`) without validating it, so anything that isn't a numpy array fails, including the pandas/polars output that `set_output` makes the estimator itself return.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import FeatureAgglomeration

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(10, 4)
fa = FeatureAgglomeration(n_clusters=2).fit(X)

fa.inverse_transform([[1.0, 2.0]])      # TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple

fa.set_output(transform="pandas")
fa.inverse_transform(fa.transform(X))   # pandas InvalidIndexError
```

### Expected Results

Same result as passing the equivalent ndarray (the docstring says X is array-like of shape (n_samples, n_clusters) or (n_clusters,)).

### Actual Results

- list: `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple`
- pandas (including the estimator's own `set_output(transform="pandas")` output): `InvalidIndexError` / `KeyError`
- polars: `DuplicateError`

A plain ndarray works.

### Versions

```shell
scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.0.6, polars 1.44.2, numpy 2.5.3 (main has the same code).
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes. I have a fix (validate with `check_array(X, ensure_2d=False)` in `inverse_transform`, plus tests for list/pandas/polars/1-D input) and would like to open the PR once this is triaged.

Found with AI assistance (Claude); I verified the repro.

`from sklearn.model_selection import *` raises ImportError since 1.8.0

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm a CS student and regular scikit-learn user, mostly through model_selection. I ran into this while star-importing the module in a notebook and traced it back to a specific commit. First time filing a bug here.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`from sklearn.model_selection import *` raises an ImportError on 1.8.0+. It worked in 1.7.2, and every other public submodule still star-imports fine.

The cause: `HalvingGridSearchCV` and `HalvingRandomSearchCV` are listed in `__all__` (in `sklearn/model_selection/__init__.py`), but the module's `__getattr__` deliberately raises ImportError for both until you import `enable_halving_search_cv`. Star-import pulls every name in `__all__`, so it hits that guard and fails. The two names were added to `__all__` in #31847 (the ruff absolute-imports cleanup); before that they weren't exported.

Impact: any notebook or script doing `from sklearn.model_selection import *` breaks on upgrade to 1.8.0, with an error that looks unrelated to what the user actually did.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import *
```

### Expected Results

Star-import succeeds like it did in 1.7.2, without exporting the experimental Halving classes.

### Actual Results

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File ".../sklearn/model_selection/__init__.py", line 100, in __getattr__
    raise ImportError(
ImportError: HalvingGridSearchCV is experimental and the API might change without any deprecation cycle. To use it, you need to explicitly import enable_halving_search_cv:
from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.10 (tags/v3.12.10:0cc8128, Apr  8 2025, 12:21:36) [MSC v.1943 64 bit (AMD64)]
   machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
          pip: 25.0.1
        numpy: 2.6.0.dev0
        scipy: 2.0.0.dev0
       pandas: 3.1.0.dev0+2081.ge909fc44ba
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
     narwhals: 2.26.0

Also reproduces on 1.8.0.
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Happy to open a PR. Plan: drop the two names from `__all__` and keep them in the `TYPE_CHECKING` import with `# noqa: F401`, the way 1.7.2 had it.

text:
BUG: Pipeline.fit_predict skips transform_input for final-step metadata

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With metadata routing enabled and `transform_input=["X_val"]`, `Pipeline.fit_predict` passes transformed training data to the final estimator but leaves `X_val` untransformed. An otherwise identical call to `Pipeline.fit` transforms `X_val` correctly.

In the reproducer, the final estimator receives `X_val = [[15.0]]` through `fit_predict`, although the fitted scaler maps that value to `[[0.0]]`. No exception is raised.

This can put training data and validation metadata in different feature spaces. An estimator that uses the metadata could therefore compute incorrect validation quantities or make different fitting decisions. Preprocessing that changes the feature count could instead cause a shape error. These are potential consequences; the reproducer demonstrates the incorrect metadata, not a production failure or incorrect predictions from a built-in estimator.

The [documented purpose of `transform_input`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html) is to transform selected metadata before the consuming step receives it, including validation data.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)


class RecordsXVal(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    def fit(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        self.X_val_seen_ = X_val
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.zeros(len(X))

    def fit_predict(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        return self.fit(X, y, X_val=X_val).predict(X)


X = np.array([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
X_val = np.array([[15.0]])

for method in ("fit", "fit_predict"):
    pipe = Pipeline(
        [
            ("scale", StandardScaler()),
            ("model", RecordsXVal().set_fit_request(X_val=True)),
        ],
        transform_input=["X_val"],
    )
    getattr(pipe, method)(X, y, X_val=X_val)
    print(
        sklearn.__version__,
        method,
        "final step received X_val =",
        pipe[-1].X_val_seen_.ravel(),
    )
```

### Expected Results

Both methods should pass the transformed validation value to the final estimator:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [0.]
```

The same is expected on 1.9.0. The scaler is fitted on `[0, 10, 20, 30]`, whose mean is `15`, so transforming `[[15.0]]` gives `[[0.0]]`.

### Actual Results

Running the reproducer separately in the two affected environments produced:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
1.9.0 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.0 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
```

No exception is raised. Only `fit_predict` passes the original validation value to the final estimator.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The likely cause is the final-step parameter handling in [`Pipeline.fit_predict`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.1/sklearn/pipeline.py):

```python
params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
```

Unlike `fit` and `fit_transform`, this does not use `_get_metadata_for_step` for the final estimator. The intermediate-step fix in [#34201](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34201/files) does not change that final-step assignment.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
+ params_last_step = self._get_metadata_for_step(
+     step_idx=len(self) - 1,
+     step_params=routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]],
+     all_params=params,
+ )
```

A regression test should assert that the final estimator receives `pipe[:-1].transform(X_val)` after `fit_predict`, with `fit` as a passing control. For example, append this assertion after the reproducer's loop:

```python
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    pipe[-1].X_val_seen_,
    pipe[:-1].transform(X_val),
)
```

This suggestion still needs validation against a patched target-version checkout and the relevant upstream tests.

        return self.fit(X, y, X_val=X_val).predict(X)


X = np.array([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
X_val = np.array([[15.0]])

for method in ("fit", "fit_predict"):
    pipe = Pipeline(
        [
            ("scale", StandardScaler()),
            ("model", RecordsXVal().set_fit_request(X_val=True)),
        ],
        transform_input=["X_val"],
    )
    getattr(pipe, method)(X, y, X_val=X_val)
    print(
        sklearn.__version__,
        method,
        "final step received X_val =",
        pipe[-1].X_val_seen_.ravel(),
    )
```

### Expected Results

Both methods should pass the transformed validation value to the final estimator:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [0.]
```

The same is expected on 1.9.0. The scaler is fitted on `[0, 10, 20, 30]`, whose mean is `15`, so transforming `[[15.0]]` gives `[[0.0]]`.

### Actual Results

Running the reproducer separately in the two affected environments produced:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
1.9.0 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.0 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
```

No exception is raised. Only `fit_predict` passes the original validation value to the final estimator.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The likely cause is the final-step parameter handling in [`Pipeline.fit_predict`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.1/sklearn/pipeline.py):

```python
params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
```

Unlike `fit` and `fit_transform`, this does not use `_get_metadata_for_step` for the final estimator. The intermediate-step fix in [#34201](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34201/files) does not change that final-step assignment.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
+ params_last_step = self._get_metadata_for_step(
+     step_idx=len(self) - 1,
+     step_params=routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]],
+     all_params=params,
+ )
```

A regression test should assert that the final estimator receives `pipe[:-1].transform(X_val)` after `fit_predict`, with `fit` as a passing control. For example, append this assertion after the reproducer's loop:

```python
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    pipe[-1].X_val_seen_,
    pipe[:-1].transform(X_val),
)
```

This suggestion still needs validation against a patched target-version checkout and the relevant upstream tests.

DOC/ENH: StandardScaler silently sets scale to 1.0 for zero-variance features with no warning

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a recent CS/AI graduate currently building a personal finance app that uses scikit-learn for some ML-based features (budgeting insights, basic predictive modeling). While setting up a local editable build to start learning the codebase and look for ways to contribute, I was testing edge cases with StandardScaler and noticed it silently returns a scale of 1.0 for zero-variance features (e.g. a single-sample fit) without any warning or documentation of this behavior. I dug into the source (_handle_zeros_in_scale) to confirm it was intentional rather than a bug, and found the public docstring doesn't mention it.

I'd like to help fix this if it's something the maintainers agree is worth addressing — happy to work on either a documentation update or a warning, whichever direction you'd prefer.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

StandardScaler.fit() silently returns a scale of 1.0 (instead of erroring or
warning) when a feature has zero or near-zero variance — e.g. a single-sample
fit, or a constant column. This is implemented via the internal
_handle_zeros_in_scale helper, but the behavior is not mentioned in the
public StandardScaler docstring or the User Guide.

Minimal reproduction:

​```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3]])  # single sample — zero variance
scaler = StandardScaler()
print(scaler.fit_transform(X))
# Output: [[0., 0., 0.]] — no warning, no error raised
​```

This could silently mask real data problems — e.g. an accidental single-row
fit, or a constant column slipping through a preprocessing pipeline —
producing all-zero output with no signal to the user that something
unusual happened.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Adding a note to the StandardScaler docstring (and the corresponding section of the User Guide at doc/modules/preprocessing.rst) explaining that when a feature has zero or near-zero variance, its scale_ is set to 1.0 rather than raising an error or leaving a zero — so the transformed output for that feature will be 0. rather than NaN or inf. This would at least make the existing behavior discoverable without changing any code.

Ridge solver is set to Cholesky even if SVD is used

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In Ridge, when the regularization is zero or too small and the covariance is non-PSD, scikit-learn will first attempt to solve the linear system using Cholesky, and if that fails, will fall back to SVD from SciPy's `lstsq`, but the `solver_` attribute will still be set as `"cholesky"`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
X, y = make_regression(n_samples=5, n_features=20, random_state=123)
X = np.r_[X, X]
y = np.r_[y, y]

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
Ridge(fit_intercept=False, alpha=0).fit(X, y).solver_
```

### Expected Results

Something along the lines of "svd" or "lstsq".

### Actual Results

'cholesky'

### Versions

```shell
Not relevant.
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

No.

text:
Sharing links from scikit-learn.org gives the wrong link

### Introduce yourself

Web Technologies Evangelist for the Safari and WebKit teams at Apple. I'm passing on a report we received about broken functionality on the scikit-learn.org website that was reported to us.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When sharing a link from a page on the scikit-learn.org website, the shared link is incorrectly formatted and loses the `.org` from the host. This is due to `.org` being missing in the OpenGraph URL meta tag:

```
<meta content="https://scikit-learn/stable/auto_examples/datasets/plot_iris_dataset.html" property="og:url"/>
```

Fixing this will fix link sharing.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

1. Load a page on the site: (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/datasets/plot_iris_dataset.html)
2. Share to Messages via the toolbar button
3. Send the link, then copy it and note that the resulting link is missing `.org`

### Expected Results

Sharing a link should result in a valid URL to the site.

### Actual Results

The link shared in the example case is: https://scikit-learn/stable/auto_examples/datasets/plot_iris_dataset.html

### Versions

```shell
# Not Applicable
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

I am passing this issue on for project maintainers to fix.

text: Incorrect random_state description in RANSACRegressor documentation ### Introduce yourself Hi! I am new to the scikit-learn community. I am a data scientist and often use `scikit-learn` for my experiments. I recently used `RANSACRegressor` and noticed a possible documentation issue. ### Describe the issue linked to the documentation The `random_state` parameter is currently documented as: `The generator used to initialize the centers`. This description appears unrelated to `RANSACRegressor` and actually related to a clustering algorithm . In the implementation, `random_state` is used with `sample_without_replacement` to randomly select data subsets during RANSAC iterations. These subsets are then used to fit candidate models. The issue also stays in the final `sklearn` documentation linked here : [ransac](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.RANSACRegressor.html. ### Suggest a potential alternative/fix Suggested correction : `random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None Controls the randomness of the data subsets selected during RANSAC iterations. Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls. See :term:`Glossary `.` I have tested the change locally, and the RANSAC test suite passes: 27 passed in 0.47s I would be happy to submit a pull request for this documentation fix if the issue is valid.

text:
Support infinite values in DecisionTree/RandomForest/ExtraTrees (now that NaN is supported)

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Hello,

I am facing a problem where the proper handling of infinite values would be helpful. Since the introduction of the support for missing values (#23595/#26391/#27966), I was wondering to what extent it would be possible to handle those.

Currently:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [np.inf], [10.0]])
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]
DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X, y)
# ValueError: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float32').
```

This is because infinite value is explicitly rejected regardless, in `BaseDecisionTree._compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask` (`sklearn/tree/_classes.py`):
A second guard in `_validate_X_predict` (same file) does the same at predict time.

```
if not np.isfinite(overall_sum):
    # Raise a ValueError in case of the presence of an infinite element.
    _assert_all_finite_element_wise(X, xp=np, allow_nan=True, **common_kwargs)
```

Both guards live on `BaseDecisionTree`, shared by all four tree classes; `RandomForest*`/`ExtraTrees*` call the same method rather than duplicating it. 

`GradientBoostingClassifier`/`Regressor` don't set `allow_nan` and aren't affected either way. Small number of call sites.

### Describe your proposed solution

The splitter already tolerates infinite values without modification. Unlike NaN, +inf/-inf are ordinary totally-ordered floats (-inf < finite < +inf), so <= comparisons already place them correctly, with no new split-evaluation logic needed like NaN required. Verified by monkeypatching out just the two guards: DecisionTreeClassifier fits and predicts correctly on +inf/-inf data, including placing a real split threshold at -inf. Checked sklearn/tree/_splitter.pyx too: thresholds are computed as feature_values[p_prev]/2.0 + feature_values[p]/2.0 (sum-of-halves, to avoid overflow on large finite values), with a fallback to feature_values[p_prev] if the result lands exactly on +INFINITY/-INFINITY. With real -inf in the data this fallback is a no-op (-inf sorts first, so the fallback value is -inf too).

check_estimators_nan_inf (the common test for this) is already skipped entirely for these estimators (gated by one allow_nan tag covering both NaN and inf), so relaxing the guard doesn't remove existing coverage, though new tests would need to be added for inf specifically. Proposal: relax the two guards (behind allow_nan or a new dedicated tag), and add that dedicated inf/NaN test coverage.

text:
Add Population Stability Index (PSI) as a model/data drift metric

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I want to detect when a feature's or a model score's distribution has shifted between two datasets (e.g. training vs. a more recent production sample). Using Population Stability Index - sum((new_pct - base_pct) * log(new_pct / base_pct)) over aligned bins/categories is a standard for doing so. 

This is one of the most common "has my model gone stale" checks in production ML monitoring, sitting next to sklearn.metrics conceptually (it's a distance/divergence metric between two empirical distributions, similar in spirit to things like scipy.stats.entropy/KL divergence that sklearn already depends on via scipy).

### Describe your proposed solution

sklearn.metrics.population_stability_index(base, new, bins=10) for continuous input (auto-binning via quantiles of base) and direct category alignment for categorical/discrete input, returning the scalar PSI (and optionally a per-bin breakdown table).

possibly also some rolling_psi method for evaluating the PSI over different time periods.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Checked scikit-learn's and statsmodels' issue trackers directly for prior discussion of PSI - found none in either (no open request, nothing closed as wontfix). Purpose-built alternatives exist as separate packages, but nothing really maintained, while PSI is old and widely used operationally.

### Additional context

Population Stability Index has been standard practice in credit scoring model monitoring since well before modern ML tooling (commonly attributed to the SAS/banking scorecard literature from the 1990s-2000s); today it's also used more broadly for feature/data drift detection outside credit scoring specifically.

text:
Add Information Value (IV) / Weight-of-Evidence binning as metric and feature-selection

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Rank a feature's predictive strength against a binary target by binning it (equal-frequency or optimized) and computing Information Value: `sum((pct_event - pct_nonevent) * log(pct_event / pct_nonevent))` over bins.

This is a standard univariate feature-screening step in binary classification, conceptually adjacent to things sklearn already ships in `sklearn.feature_selection` (`mutual_info_classif`, `f_classif`, chi2) as a way to rank/filter features before modeling. Notably this metric does not depends on imbalance. 

### Describe your proposed solution

'sklearn.metric.IV(X,y, bins=10) would be useful for establishing Information value. Then 'sklearn.feature_selection.information_value(X, y, bins=10)' returning per-feature IV, using equal-frequency quantile binning by default (fast, matches the common textbook definition).


### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Checked scikit-learn's issue tracker for "Information Value" and "Weight of Evidence" - found nothing (no open request, no closed-as-declined). The realistic existing option is `optbinning`, a purpose-built, actively maintained package that solves actual bin optimization (via a CP/MIP solver) rather than plain quantile cuts.

IV/WOE binning is old and widely used, but specifically within credit-scoring-style binary classification rather than general ML - similar concern to the adjacent PSI request I'm also filing. Raising it mainly to get a maintainer judgment on record, since I couldn't find this discussed anywhere in scikit-learn's history.



### Additional context

`mutual_info_classif` already covers "how predictive is this feature" in a distribution-agnostic way; IV specifically gives interpretable, additive-across-bins output that credit-risk practitioners rely on for regulatory model documentation, which is the main reason it persists as a distinct metric rather than being subsumed by mutual information in that field.

PolynomialCountSketch.bitHash_ docstring says dtype=float32 but is actually int64

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for general ML work. I found this while cross-checking
the `PolynomialCountSketch` docs against its implementation for an unrelated
performance PR (#34919) and noticed the `bitHash_` attribute's documented
dtype doesn't match what the code actually produces.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`PolynomialCountSketch`'s `bitHash_` attribute is documented as:

```
bitHash_ : ndarray of shape (degree, n_features), dtype=float32
    Array with random entries in {+1, -1}, used to represent
    the 2-wise independent hash functions for Count Sketch computation.
```

but it is actually set with:

```python
self.bitHash_ = random_state.choice(a=[-1, 1], size=(self.degree, n_features))
```

`numpy.random.RandomState.choice` with an integer array `a=[-1, 1]` and no
explicit `dtype` produces an integer array, not `float32`. This has been the
case since the class was introduced (scikit-learn/scikit-learn#13003, 2019),
so it is not a regression, just a docstring that was never accurate.

User-facing impact is limited (the attribute is internal-ish and the class
still works correctly), but anyone relying on the documented dtype — for
example writing code that assumes `bitHash_.astype(np.float32, copy=False)`
is a no-op, or reasoning about memory usage from the docstring — would be
misled.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.kernel_approximation import PolynomialCountSketch

X = np.random.RandomState(0).random_sample((50, 20))
ps = PolynomialCountSketch(degree=2, n_components=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print(ps.bitHash_.dtype)
```

### Expected Results

```
float32
```
(matching the docstring)

### Actual Results

```
int64
```

### Versions

```
System:
    python: 3.14.6 (v3.14.6:c63aec69bd5, Jun 10 2026, 08:07:54) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)]
executable: /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.14/bin/python3
   machine: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
          pip: 26.1.2
   setuptools: 83.0.0
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: 3.3.0
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.25.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

I'd be happy to open a PR to fix the docstring to say the actual dtype
(`int64`, or more precisely whatever `numpy.random.RandomState.choice`
returns for an integer input array) once this is triaged.

Documentation: Incorrect description of statistic computed by MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Pradip, a Computer Engineering student and I’m currently learning and working with Python and machine learning. I use scikit-learn for learning and implementing machine learning algorithms and preprocessing techniques.

While going through the `MaxAbsScaler` documentation and source code, I noticed a discrepancy in the `partial_fit()` docstring. I’m opening this issue to clarify the documentation and make it consistent with the actual implementation.


### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` currently states that the data is used to compute the **"per-feature minimum and maximum"**.

However, `MaxAbsScaler` computes the **maximum absolute value** for each feature and stores it in `max_abs_`.

For example:

```python
X = [[-2, 5],
     [-3, 1]]
```

For the first feature:

```text
minimum = -3
maximum = -2
maximum absolute value = 3
```

`MaxAbsScaler` uses `3` as the scaling value. It does not use the minimum and maximum as separate statistics.

The implementation reflects this:

```python
max_abs = xpx.nanmax(xp.abs(X), axis=0, xp=xp)
```

Therefore, the current wording may confuse users into thinking that `MaxAbsScaler` computes and uses both the minimum and maximum values independently.

This also appears inconsistent with the class-level documentation, which describes the scaler in terms of the **maximum absolute value**.

I believe this is a documentation-only issue and does not require any change to the underlying algorithm.


### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I suggest updating the `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` from:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature minimum and maximum
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

to:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature maximum absolute value
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

This would make the `partial_fit()` documentation accurately reflect the statistic computed by the implementation and remain consistent with the class-level documentation.

balanced_accuracy_score(adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the NaN filter

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a data scientist in Toronto working on forecasting and causal inference. I've recently started contributing to scikit-learn — I have an open PR at #34888 (array API support for ShrunkCovariance) — and I found this while looking into #33712, where I was trying to work out which of two distinct undefined cases in balanced_accuracy_score that issue refers to. This one turned out to be independent of it, so I'm filing it separately.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

balanced_accuracy_score(..., adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the internal NaN filter. The adjusted score is bounded — it spans [-1, 1], reaching -1 only at n_classes=2 — so -inf is outside the documented range of the metric.

This surfaces in cross-validation on small or imbalanced folds, where a fold can easily contain a single class. One -inf propagates through any mean over folds, turning the whole aggregate into -inf and silently destroying an otherwise valid CV score. The related nan case is at least absorbed by nan-aware aggregation; -inf is not.

Mechanism: n_classes is read after the NaN filter at _classification.py:2940, so when one class survives, chance = 1 / 1 and `score /= 1 - chance` at line 2946 divides by zero. The np.errstate guard wraps the per-class division only, not this one, and has been scoped that way since the original commit (e888c0d65cf, "ENH multiclass balanced accuracy" #10587, 2018) — the guard and the unguarded division were introduced together.

This is separate from #33712: it predates it and reproduces without touching replace_undefined_by.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

# Case 1
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], adjusted=True))

# Case 2
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], adjusted=True))
```

## Expected Results

A value within the documented range of the adjusted metric, [-1, 1]. A score documented as bounded should not return -inf.

## Actual Results

On scikit-learn 1.9.0 (installed from PyPI), case 1 returns nan:

```
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:614: UserWarning: A single label was found in 'y_true' and 'y_pred'. For the confusion matrix to have the correct shape, use the 'labels' parameter to pass all known labels.
  warnings.warn(
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2946: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in scalar divide
  score /= 1 - chance
nan
```

Case 2 returns -inf:

```
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2939: UserWarning: y_pred contains classes not in y_true
  warnings.warn("y_pred contains classes not in y_true")
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2946: RuntimeWarning: divide by zero encountered in scalar divide
  score /= 1 - chance
-inf
```

Both RuntimeWarnings come from the same unguarded statement at line 2946. The texts differ — "invalid value" for case 1, "divide by zero" for case 2 — which maps onto the nan/-inf split: case 1 is 0/0, case 2 is -0.333/0.

Also reproduces unchanged on main (1.10.dev0), where the filter is at line 2969 and the division at line 2975.

text: [BUG] `compute_class_weight` coerces class labels to int in 1.9, breaking dict lookup for string labels ### Introduce yourself hi, I am a core developer for the aeon toolkit and an academic at the university of Southampton. I found this bug when trying to raise our upper bound for scikit https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon/pull/3787 For context, we have a range of algorithms that use scikit components, in this case the `ExtraTreeClassifier` and `RandomForestClassifier`. We also maintain a range of data archives including the UCR archive, hosted here http://timeseriesclassification.com/ Our classification data always loads class values as strings, so for example, "1"/"2" or "Run"/"Jump". The basic problem is that relevant parts of scikit 1.9 now always parse class value strings to integers, leading to dictionary errors. I had a good look and couldnt see this issue, sorry if its been fixed already. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact In 1.9, fitting a forest ensemble with `class_weight="balanced"` raises `ValueError` when the class labels are strings that happen to parse as integers ("1", "2", ...). The same code works in 1.8 and earlier. Labels that are genuine integers, or strings that do not parse as integers ("a", "b"), are unaffected. The problem comes from a coercion added to the user-defined-dictionary branch of compute_class_weight in #32644 (commit 9ca766b, "FEA Add array API support for LogisticRegression with LBFGS"): ```python for i, c in enumerate(classes): try: c = int(c) except ValueError: # `classes` contains strings c = str(c) if c in class_weight: ``` The intent looks like normalising array scalars to Python scalars so that dict lookup by key works under a non-numpy namespace. But int("1") succeeds, so it never reaches the except clause that would have preserved the string. That branch is reached even though the user asked for "balanced", because `BaseForest._validate_y_class_weight` does not pass "balanced" straight through. It round-trips (sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py:861): ```python # Computing class_weight (dict or list) for the "balanced" option. class_weight_k_vect = compute_class_weight("balanced", classes=self.classes_[k], ...) class_weight_k = {key: val for (key, val) in zip(self.classes_[k], class_weight_k_vect)} ... expanded_class_weight = compute_sample_weight(class_weight, y_original) ``` It first expands "balanced" into an explicit dict keyed by the original labels — {"1": 1.0, "2": 1.0}, string keys — and then feeds that dict back in. The second call goes through the dictionary branch, the keys are coerced to int, every lookup fails, and all classes are reported as unweighted. Estimators that pass "balanced" directly to `compute_class_weight (DecisionTreeClassifier, RidgeClassifierCV, SVC, ...)` take the dedicated `elif class_weight == "balanced"` branch, which uses a LabelEncoder and never coerces, so they are not affected. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(20, 5) y = np.array(["1"] * 10 + ["2"] * 10) # string labels that parse as integers RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=5, class_weight="balanced").fit(X, y) ```` Or against compute_class_weight directly, without the forest: ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_class_weight compute_class_weight( {"1": 1.0, "2": 1.0}, classes=np.array(["1", "2"]), y=np.array(["1", "2", "1"]) ) ``` ### Expected Results Expected Results Fits without error, as in 1.8.0 and earlier. The direct compute_class_weight call returns array([1., 1.]). ### Actual Results ```python-traceback Traceback (most recent call last): File "repro.py", line 7, in RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=5, class_weight="balanced").fit(X, y) File "sklearn/base.py", line 1403, in wrapper return fit_method(estimator, *args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py", line 393, in fit y, expanded_class_weight = self._validate_y_class_weight(y, sample_weight) File "sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py", line 879, in _validate_y_class_weight expanded_class_weight = compute_sample_weight(class_weight, y_original) File "sklearn/utils/_param_validation.py", line 191, in wrapper return func(*args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/utils/class_weight.py", line 236, in compute_sample_weight weight_k = compute_class_weight( File "sklearn/utils/_param_validation.py", line 191, in wrapper return func(*args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/utils/class_weight.py", line 117, in compute_class_weight raise ValueError( ValueError: The classes, [1, 2], are not in class_weight ``` The message is also misleading: it reports the classes as [1, 2] (post-coercion integers) when the real classes are the strings ["1", "2"], which are the dict keys. A mixed example shows the failure is per-label and driven purely by whether int() succeeds — with classes ["0", "a"] only "0" is reported: This effects both ExtraTreesClassifier and RandomForestClassifier ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.12.9 [MSC v.1942 64 bit (AMD64)] machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.9.0 pip: 26.1.2 setuptools: 82.0.1 numpy: 2.4.6 scipy: 1.18.0 Cython: None pandas: 2.2.3 matplotlib: 3.10.1 joblib: 1.4.2 threadpoolctl: 3.5.0 ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug yes I would be happy to, I would not convert strings to ints at all, leave them as string and would not use a try ... except block in this context and avoid the round trip, but would need to look more closely, claude suggests this fix (and has helped me pin this down) ```python Convert the labels to Python scalars without altering their values, rather than parsing them. move_to is already imported and used earlier in the same function: for i, c in enumerate(classes): - try: - c = int(c) - except ValueError: # `classes` contains strings - c = str(c) + # convert to python scalars so that lookup by dict key works for any + # array namespace, without altering the label values themselves + for i, c in enumerate(move_to(classes, xp=np, device="cpu").tolist()): if c in class_weight: tolist() maps each element to its natural Python type — str stays str, int stays int — and both hash-match the user's dict keys, which is what the array-API port needed. Unlike int(), it never alters a label's value, so it cannot introduce this class of mismatch for any label type. ``` A narrower guard such as if not isinstance(c, str) around the existing int() call also fixes it, which is probably what I would do, but I obviously dont have the wider picture.

A mixed example shows the failure is per-label and driven purely by whether int() succeeds — with classes ["0", "a"] only "0" is reported: This effects both ExtraTreesClassifier and RandomForestClassifier ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.12.9 [MSC v.1942 64 bit (AMD64)] machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.9.0 pip: 26.1.2 setuptools: 82.0.1 numpy: 2.4.6 scipy: 1.18.0 Cython: None pandas: 2.2.3 matplotlib: 3.10.1 joblib: 1.4.2 threadpoolctl: 3.5.0 ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug yes I would be happy to, I would not convert strings to ints at all, leave them as string and would not use a try ... except block in this context and avoid the round trip, but would need to look more closely, claude suggests this fix (and has helped me pin this down) ```python Convert the labels to Python scalars without altering their values, rather than parsing them. move_to is already imported and used earlier in the same function: for i, c in enumerate(classes): - try: - c = int(c) - except ValueError: # `classes` contains strings - c = str(c) + # convert to python scalars so that lookup by dict key works for any + # array namespace, without altering the label values themselves + for i, c in enumerate(move_to(classes, xp=np, device="cpu").tolist()): if c in class_weight: tolist() maps each element to its natural Python type — str stays str, int stays int — and both hash-match the user's dict keys, which is what the array-API port needed. Unlike int(), it never alters a label's value, so it cannot introduce this class of mismatch for any label type. ``` A narrower guard such as if not isinstance(c, str) around the existing int() call also fixes it, which is probably what I would do, but I obviously dont have the wider picture.

text:
Investigation: conda-forge scikit-learn slower than PyPI (ExtraTrees case)

While looking at [builds comparison results](https://probabl-ai.github.io/scikit-learn-benchmarks/builds_comparison.html) from my benchmarks (https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks), I noticed `ExtraTrees*.fit` was often ~25% slower on conda-forge builds of
scikit-learn 1.9.0 than on PyPI wheels.

Two distinct bugs were found along the way; only the second one explains the slowdown:

1. **O3 vs O2** (documented in #34865): `-O3` in meson doesn't survive an environment `CFLAGS` that also sets `-O2` (which conda-forge's compiler activation does).

2. **Version of `glibc`** (cause of the slowdown): conda-forge compiles scikit-learn against a `sysroot_linux-64=2.17` (glibc 2.17, from 2012-12-25). That old glibc's `<math.h>` defines the `isnan()` macro as a dispatch to glibc-internal `__isnanf`/`__isnan` functions instead of `__builtin_isnan*`. GCC can't recognize or inline those, so `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx`'s `isnan(value)` calls — sitting in the hottest loop of tree-building (`find_min_max`, `partition_samples`) — become genuine non-inlined function calls. This is `fit`-specific (confirmed: `predict`, which doesn't call these functions, shows no slowdown) and fully reproduced from source once the exact sysroot was pinned.


This is very likely **not scikit-learn-specific**: any conda-forge package with a hot-loop `isnan()`/`isinf()` call is plausibly exposed the same way.

~~=> TODO: Open an issue in conda-forge~~ Done: I posted a comment here: https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compiler-activation-feedstock/issues/108

### Proposed fix

Replace `from libc.math cimport isnan` / `isnan(value)` in `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` (and any other tree/HGB hot loop doing the same) with the self-inequality NaN test `value != value`. Pure comparison, nothing to inline, immune to this class of bug on any compiler/libc, forever.

### Root cause, in detail

*(pure LLM write-up)*

<details>

`sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` (`DensePartitioner.find_min_max`, `.partition_samples`) and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` call `isnan(value)` on `float32_t` data, via `from libc.math cimport isnan`. This runs once per sample per feature scan during `fit`; never during `predict`.

The feedstock's CI pin file (`.ci_support/linux_64_python3.12.____cpython.yaml` at the 1.9.0 release commit) sets `c_stdlib: sysroot`, `c_stdlib_version: '2.17'`. That sysroot's `math.h` has:

```c
#  define isnan(x) \
     (sizeof (x) == sizeof (float) ? __isnanf (x) \
      : sizeof (x) == sizeof (double) ? __isnan (x) : __isnanl (x))
```

Once the preprocessor expands this, the identifier `isnan` is gone from
the translation unit — GCC has nothing left to recognize as a builtin, so
`__isnanf` (an ordinary external glibc symbol, not a compiler intrinsic)
gets a real out-of-line call. Modern glibc instead defines `isnan(x)` as
`__builtin_isnan(x)` directly, which GCC folds to 2 instructions
(`ucomiss`/`setp`). PyPI/manylinux wheels don't hit this because they're
built with devtoolset-style toolchains: modern compiler *and* modern
headers, achieving old-system compatibility via glibc *symbol versioning*
at link time rather than by literally compiling against old headers.

Confirmed end to end:
- `perf`-profiled real installed PyPI vs conda-forge packages
  (`ExtraTreesRegressor.fit`, `n_features=30`): conda-forge spends 12.6% of
  samples in `__isnanf` alone; PyPI doesn't show it in the top 15 at all.
- Disassembled both real `.so` files directly: conda-forge's
  `find_min_max` has `call *0x1791f(%rip)  # <__isnanf@GLIBC_2.2.5>`;
  PyPI's has no call at all.
- Reproduced from source: rebuilding the actual v1.9.0 tag with the exact
  matching GCC (14.3.0-19, confirmed via the real binary's own
  `.comment` section) reproduced nothing *until* `sysroot_linux-64=2.17`
  was pinned explicitly (every environment had otherwise resolved the
  latest default, 2.39) — at which point the non-inlined call and the
  larger function size reappeared byte-for-byte.
- Same `isnan()` call pattern, same functions, confirmed still present on
  current `main` (the categorical-feature/Breiman-shortcut work added
  since 1.9.0 didn't touch this code path — `find_min_max` compiles to the
  identical byte size on both).

</details>

### Everything else that was tried and ruled out

Before finding the sysroot, a long list of variables was controlled for one at a time and **did not** reproduce the real-world gap when rebuilding from source with the real conda-forge `gcc_linux-64`/`gxx_linux-64` toolchain:

<details>

- `-O2` vs `-O3` in isolation (~1.7% effect — this is the Meson bug above)
- `-march=nocona -mtune=haswell` vs no override
- GCC version: 16.2.0, 13.4.0, and the exact `14.3.0-19` patch build
  (pinning `gcc_impl_linux-64`/`gxx_impl_linux-64`/`binutils_impl_linux-64`
  precisely, since `gcc_impl_linux-64` has its own build-number sequence
  independent of the `gcc_linux-64` wrapper)
- Cython version (real binary uses 3.2.5; early rebuilds had picked up
  3.3.0 by default — controlled for, no effect)
- Exact v1.9.0 source tag vs current `main`
- Editable install vs literal `python -m build -w` wheel build (matching
  `build.sh` exactly)
- `-fno-merge-constants` (the extra flag conda-forge adds under
  `CONDA_BUILD=1`)
- joblib version, core-count detection, BLAS threading config — all
  identical between real PyPI and conda-forge installs

</details>

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'll open the PR very soon.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm Daniel and I use Scikit-learn both in private projects and at work. I work as a Data Scientist and currently building a personal project.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

So I am working on a data classification project and trying to use one-hot encoding within a pipeline.  I have organised my columns based on the needed impute through SimpleImputer (mean and most frequent). Simple imputer was able to impute where its needed and ignore non-missing columns but One-Hot always encode everything regardless of dtype. And I couldn't avoid that without re-editing my columns even though my groupings work well without repetition. 

### Describe your proposed solution

My proposed solution is to add a `skip` kwarg so the user can select the columns to skip during the process. I believe better solutions could be developed but thats what I am currently thinking.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Could probably use `make_column_selector` but the user still has to manually encode at some point.

### Additional context

_No response_
